# Mahāsamaya Sutta (DN 20 (PTS DN ii 253))

**ID:** DN 20 (PTS DN ii 253)  
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Mahāsamaya Sutta  
**PTS:** DN ii 253  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0102m.mul6.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0102m.mul6.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāsamaya Sutta* ("The Great Congregation", DN 20) is the twentieth discourse of the *Dīghanikāya*, set in the Great Wood (*Mahāvana*) at Kapilavatthu in the Sakyan territory [Skilling 1993]. The word *samaya* in the title denotes a meeting or "concourse", explained by the commentary as a "great assembly" (*mahāsamūha*) [Bodhi 2000]. The narrative background recounts how the Buddha mediated a conflict between the Sakyans and Koliyans over the waters of the Rohiṇī River, after which five hundred youths went forth and attained arahantship, assembling before the Buddha on the full-moon night of Jeṭṭhamūla [Bodhi 2000]. When deities from across the realms gathered to pay homage, the Buddha uttered verses naming and describing the assembled gods, yakkhas, and spirits [Williams 2000]. Providing one of the most extensive catalogues of deities in early Indian Buddhism, these verses became a central protective text (*paritta* / *rakṣā*), commonly chanted throughout Theravādin traditions and included among the recitations of the *Catubhāṇavāra* [Holz 2022].

Direct Sanskrit parallels, titled *Mahāsamājasūtra*, are preserved among Central Asian manuscript fragments edited by Ernst Waldschmidt [Nakamura 1980; Skilling 1992]. Two distinct Tibetan translations exist in the Kanjur: an early translation of the Mūlasarvāstivādin *Mahāsamājasūtra* (D 34) executed around 800 CE by Jinamitra, Prajñāvarman, and Ye shes sde, and a 14th-century translation by Ānandaśrī and Nyi ma rgyal mtshan that translates directly from a Theravādin text and preserves the title *Mahāsamaya-sūtra* [Skilling 1992; Skilling 1993]. Within the Pali canon, the opening prose and verse portions are identical with SN 1.37 in the *Devatā Saṁyutta*, and passages are closely shared with the *Āṭānāṭiya Sutta* (DN 32) and the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16) [Bodhi 2000].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: DA 19 大會; SF 108; SF 140 Mahāsamāja; SF 242 Mahāsamāja; SF 282 Mahāsamāja; SF 55; SHT Sutta 8; T 19 大三摩惹; D 34 འདུས་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་མདོ། (Mahāsamaya-sūtra)
- Passage-level parallels: SA2 105 集會; SA 1192 集會; SN 1.37 Samayasutta

**Sources**

- [Bodhi 2000] Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Connected Discourses of the Buddha (2000) — Commentarial narrative background on the Rohiṇī dispute, gloss on samaya/mahāsamūha, and parallel with SN 1.37.
- [Holz 2022] Holz, The Bhadrakarātrī-sūtra: Apotropaic Scriptures in Early Indian Buddhism — Details on paritta/rakṣā status, Catubhāṇavāra inclusion, and comparison with mahāsūtras.
- [Nakamura 1980] Hajime Nakamura, Indian Buddhism: A Survey With Bibliographical Notes (1980) — Reference to Waldschmidt's edition of Sanskrit Mahāsamājasūtra fragments and Miyasaka's comparative study.
- [Skilling 1992] Peter Skilling, 'Kanjur Titles and Colophons' in PIATS 6 (1992) — Sanskrit title Mahāsamājasūtra, Tibetan versions, and Ānandaśrī's 14th-century translation from Pali.
- [Skilling 1993] Peter Skilling, 'Theravādin Literature in Tibetan Translation' — Discourse setting at Kapilavatthu Mahāvana, translators of the Mūlasarvāstivādin Kanjur text, and Miyasaka's edition.
- [Williams 2000] Paul Williams (ed.), Buddhism: Critical Concepts in Religious Studies, Vol. 1 — Discussion of deities listed in the Mahāsamaya-sutta and Sanskrit/Tibetan parallels.
